rv.q: “Inside” interests us at first, bleak sight.
There's something hypnotic about the whole exercise.
A brutally beautiful fable about how writers live to write-and then forget to live.
As played in this gorgeous piece of theater by Mary Louise Parker — and, heaven forfend, what a complete performance!
We started by watching two damaged souls, portrayed with exquisite tenderness and edge, moving toward something like grace.
Directed with exquisite feeling and precision by David Cromer, this intimate drama manages to be both literary and rivetingly theatrical.

Inside is engrossing the way a good novel can be: It invites imaginative engagement, and it keeps you off balance with a steady stream of surprises as Bella’s and Christopher’s narratives—fictional and real—find an elegant equipoise.
As with many of Rapp’s prior plays, I did not find “Inside” to be a wholly credible reflection of even the direst extremes of human experience.

All in all, it’s a magical evening from Rapp, Cromer, and the altogether mesmerizing Parker and Hochman.
“Inside” is absolutely riveting theater.
Rapp’s work is hypnotic and intense, a love letter to the written word in an age of cyber and digital communication.
On Broadway every once in a while writing, acting, directing and the technical production come together to profound, memorable effect.
Her beautifully understated, deeply felt portrayal of Bella grounds the play in its own reality, even if one can possibly argue about how “real” what we’ve seen on stage turns out to be.
Happily, under David Cromer's unfussy, unassertive direction, this is one of her best performances ever.

But it feels far more literary than theatrical and I think, in the end, even with Parker's superlative performance, "Inside" is more suited to being read than seen or heard.
It is difficult to predict if this is a radical piece of theatere a pretentious production.
Tomei had to struggle against a troubling application of The Rose Tattoo in order for her to showcase her talented wisdom of characterization.

For all the play’s loquacious discussions of writing, books and authors, language, cancer, suicide, and, yes, sex, it’s difficult to become fully invested in Bella and Christopher, who seem more literary creations than flesh and blood.

cn.t: Critics praise Parker's magnetic performance and Rapp's literary thriller, though some find it too cerebral and poorly suited to Studio 54's large space. The intimate two-hander divides reviewers on its dark, meta-fictional ambitions.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
